title: Waiting, or not waiting
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain what a blocking call does to your program, switch a descriptor to non-blocking mode, and handle the error that non-blocking mode introduces without turning your program into a busy loop.

blocks.text: By default, read() on a socket with no data waits. The thread stops, uses no CPU, and resumes when something arrives. That is blocking, and for a program doing one thing at a time it is exactly right. The moment a program has to attend to two connections, it becomes a problem — because while it waits on one, it cannot notice the other.
What blocking costs, and what it does not

rows: The call returns immediately with an error meaning 'not now'
None, if you wait properly; all of it if you loop
Every call needs a 'not ready' branch
One thread can watch them all

blocks.title: Blocking is not wasteful in itself
blocks.text: A blocked thread consumes no CPU — the scheduler simply does not run it, exactly as the operating systems course described. What it consumes is a thread, and threads have a memory cost and a switching cost. That is the real limit: not that waiting is expensive, but that having ten thousand threads waiting is.

blocks.caption: Setting non-blocking mode without disturbing other flags
lines: /* Read the existing flags and add to them. Setting O_NONBLOCK on its own
would clear everything else that was set. */

blocks.text: On a non-blocking descriptor, a read with no data available returns -1 and sets errno to EAGAIN. The Linux manual states that EAGAIN and EWOULDBLOCK have the same value on all architectures, so testing for either is correct there — but portable code tests for both, because the standard permits them to differ. Neither is a failure: it is the normal answer to 'is there anything?' when there is not, and your code must treat it as a distinct case rather than as an error.

blocks.caption: The three outcomes every non-blocking read has
lines: ssize_t n = read(fd, buf, sizeof buf);
/* got n bytes — remember it may be fewer than a whole message */
/* nothing available right now — NOT an error */
/* a signal interrupted the call — just try again */
/* a real error: connection reset, and so on */

blocks.title: Non-blocking alone gives you a busy loop, not efficiency
blocks.text: Making a descriptor non-blocking and then calling read in a tight loop burns an entire core asking 'anything yet?' millions of times a second. It is slower and far more wasteful than the blocking version it replaced. Non-blocking mode is only half of a design — the other half is a call that sleeps until at least one descriptor is ready, which is the subject of the next lesson.

This is the half people forget. If the receiver is slow, the buffers between you fill up, and a blocking write waits until there is room. A non-blocking write returns EAGAIN, or writes only part of what you asked — which means your code must track how much was actually written and send the rest later.

blocks.caption: A partial write is normal and must be handled
lines: ssize_t n = write(fd, buf + sent, len - sent);
if (n < 0 && (errno == EAGAIN || errno == EWOULDBLOCK)) break;  /* try later */
/* Assuming write() sends everything is the same class of bug as
assuming read() returns a whole message. */

blocks.text: Between waiting forever and not waiting at all, a socket can be given a receive or send timeout. The call blocks, but only for a bounded time, and then returns with EAGAIN. For a client that needs to give up on an unresponsive server, this is often simpler than full non-blocking code.

blocks.title: Feel the difference
steps: Write a program that connects to a listening port and calls read() once, then prints the result
Start a listener that accepts but sends nothing: nc -l 9000
Run your program — it should hang in read(), and top should show it using no CPU
Confirm with: cat /proc/<pid>/status | grep State    (it should be sleeping)
Now set O_NONBLOCK before the read and run it again — it should return immediately
Print errno with perror and confirm you see 'Resource temporarily unavailable'
Wrap that read in a tight loop and watch CPU usage go to 100% of one core
Add a receive timeout with setsockopt SO_RCVTIMEO instead, and confirm it returns after the timeout
blocks.expected: A blocking read that sleeps at zero CPU, a non-blocking read that returns EAGAIN instantly, and a busy loop that pins a core. Seeing that third state is the point: non-blocking without a readiness mechanism is worse than what it replaced, which is exactly why the next lesson exists.

cheatsheet: Blocking: the call waits; the thread sleeps and uses no CPU
The cost of blocking is a thread per connection, not CPU while waiting
fcntl F_GETFL then F_SETFL with flags | O_NONBLOCK — never set O_NONBLOCK alone
On a non-blocking descriptor, no data gives -1 with errno EAGAIN (same as EWOULDBLOCK on Linux)
EAGAIN is not an error; EINTR means retry; anything else is a real failure
Every read has four outcomes: data, peer closed, not ready, real error
write can block too, and a partial write is normal — track how much was sent
Non-blocking plus a tight loop burns a core and is worse than blocking
SO_RCVTIMEO gives a bounded wait, which is often enough for a client

checkpoint.prompt: A blocking read waits ten seconds for data. How much CPU does the thread use during that time?

choices.B: None — a blocked thread is not scheduled at all

checkpoint.explanation: Blocking is cheap in CPU terms. What it costs is a thread, which has a memory and switching cost — and that is what limits how many connections this model can handle.

checkpoint.prompt: read() on a non-blocking socket returns -1 with errno EAGAIN. What should your code do?

choices.B: Treat it as 'nothing available yet' and come back later — it is not an error
choices.D: Report a failure to the user

checkpoint.explanation: It is the normal answer when there is no data. Retrying immediately in a loop is the busy-wait mistake; the correct next step is to wait for readiness, which the next lesson covers.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is setting O_NONBLOCK with fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, O_NONBLOCK) wrong?

choices.A: O_NONBLOCK cannot be set with fcntl
choices.B: It replaces all the flags instead of adding one, clearing anything else that was set
choices.C: It needs to be done before connect

checkpoint.explanation: Read the current flags with F_GETFL and OR the new one in. This is a small bug that produces confusing behaviour much later.

checkpoint.prompt: Your non-blocking server uses 100% of one core while idle. What is the most likely cause?

choices.B: It calls read in a tight loop instead of waiting for readiness

checkpoint.explanation: Non-blocking mode is only half a design. Without a call that sleeps until a descriptor is ready, the program spends every cycle asking whether anything has arrived.
